Quantum Optics Lab - Dual MOT Apparatus

Undergraduate research on laser cooling and trapping of ultracold rubidium atoms, working toward a Bose-Einstein condensate.

ROLEUndergraduate Researcher

MOT optics table, science chamber

Why ultracold atoms

At room temperature, atoms move at roughly 350 m/s. Cool them enough and their quantum wave-like behavior starts to show - cool them further, into the nanokelvin regime, and a cloud of bosons can condense into a single coherent matter wave: a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC). BECs are useful for quantum computation, rotational and gravitational sensing, and precision measurement.

Our lab's apparatus gets there through a chain of steps - laser cooling, magneto-optical trapping, evaporative cooling, and finally condensation - using a dual-chamber magneto-optical trap (MOT) system to collect and cool rubidium atoms.

The two-chamber design

A source chamber holds a 2D MOT that collects large numbers of atoms from a rubidium getter source at around 10⁻⁹ Torr, then pushes them through to a science chamber. There, a 3D MOT captures the atoms at ultra-high vacuum - around 10⁻¹¹ Torr - for the long trap lifetimes the experiment needs, with optical access for the dipole trap laser and imaging.

My contribution

My work on this project spans setup, electronics, and design. A lot of the day-to-day was hands-on: setting up and aligning the optics table, soldering circuit boards, and wiring up breadboard prototypes to test voltage and current flow as we automated parts of the experiment.

Optics table setup

I helped build out and align the optics table itself, the beam paths, mounts, and mirrors that make up the physical trapping setup shown above.

Electronics & automation

I got hands-on with the experiment's electronics: soldering circuit boards and starting with breadboard prototypes to test voltage and current flow before anything went into the permanent build. That electro-mechanical integration work, alongside the optical sensors, photodetectors, CCD cameras, lock-in amplifiers, and servo controllers used for imaging and laser frequency stabilization, gave me a working foundation in electronics I didn't have going in.

On the software side, I modified our Labscript (Python) code to support experimental automation, spectroscopy data acquisition, and data processing for the laser cooling sequence, including analyzing saturation spectroscopy and Doppler-broadened signals to verify laser lock stability and support servo controller tuning for closed-loop feedback.

Precision fixtures

Beam geometry in the magneto-optical trap has to be precise, the trapping beams need to intersect at the right angles and positions for the trap to work reliably. I designed a couple of the fixtures that hold that geometry in place, including an optical alignment fixture and a mounting plate, to make alignment repeatable so the setup didn't have to be re-tuned by hand from scratch every time.

Detection & what's next

We detect and characterize the trapped atoms through both fluorescence and absorption imaging, which lets us measure the temperature of the atom cloud and the lifetime of the ultracold sample. The image above came out of an absorption-imaging pipeline I built in Python.

Current work is aimed at all-optical trapping and evaporative cooling, using a focused 1064 nm fiber laser (IPG Photonics YLR-100-1064-LP, ~40 µm beam waist, ~2 mK calculated trap depth) to hold the coldest atoms and evaporate away the hottest ones, cooling the remaining sample toward the ~100 nK threshold where Bose-Einstein condensation happens.
